Windows package registration.Explanation: The identity Windows registered for this installed package. The family groups versions; the full name identifies a particular version and architecture.

Installed package metadata.Explanation: Display information, install location, and dates reported by Windows for this package.

Package health and deployment status.Explanation: Windows deployment flags describe availability, integrity, licensing, and dependency issues. These are package status signals, not a diagnosis of the app's behavior.

Resolved installed dependencies.Explanation: Dependencies supply shared components; device-family declarations define supported Windows versions. A Windows App SDK dependency alone does not prove that the app uses WinUI 3.

Dependencies and target device families.Explanation: Dependencies supply shared components; device-family declarations define supported Windows versions. A Windows App SDK dependency alone does not prove that the app uses WinUI 3.

Registry and filesystem virtualization.Explanation: Packaging can redirect registry and file writes into private app storage. Runtime, trust, and explicit manifest overrides affect this behavior.

Selected application.Explanation: Application declarations identify executable and activation entry points. Runtime and trust describe how Windows starts and isolates an app; they do not identify its UI framework.

Application activation and isolation.Explanation: Application declarations identify executable and activation entry points. Runtime and trust describe how Windows starts and isolates an app; they do not identify its UI framework.

Package identity and architecture.Explanation: Name, publisher, version, and architecture establish package identity. These are installation identifiers rather than editable preferences.

Package properties.Explanation: Publisher and display metadata describe the package. Resource references may be resolved by Windows at runtime.

Resources and languages.Explanation: Resource declarations describe language and scale variants. Installed resource packs are candidates; this view does not determine the variant selected at runtime.

Capabilities and permissions.Explanation: Capabilities declare access the package requests. A declaration does not prove that access has been granted or used.

Metadata.Explanation: Build or tooling metadata accompanies the package. Its meaning is defined by the producing tool and namespace; it is not an application setting.

PhoneIdentity.Explanation: Legacy phone identity declarations support compatibility with older Windows phone packaging. They do not establish that this app currently runs on a phone.

All applications and app extensions.Explanation: Applications and extensions declare Windows integration, including protocol handlers, file associations, and background activation.

Package extensions.Explanation: Applications and extensions declare Windows integration, including protocol handlers, file associations, and background activation.

Manifest namespaces and compatibility.Explanation: Namespaces identify schema families and versions. Compatibility declarations tell Windows how to interpret supported or ignorable extensions.

Default.Explanation: These are declarations from the package manifest. Their meaning depends on the element and its XML namespace; the original details are available below.
